cues.text: Let us turn now to graph databases, which is section four of this chapter.
A graph is built from two kinds of things: vertices, which are also called nodes, and edges, which are also called relationships.
Nodes represent entities, the things you care about, such as a patient, a clinic or a member of staff.
Edges connect those nodes.
An edge can have a direction, so it points from one node to another.
It can have a type, which says what kind of relationship it is.
And it can have properties of its own, which are extra pieces of information attached to the relationship.
Nodes can be organised too.
Labels classify nodes, so a label tells you what category a node belongs to, while properties store the attributes of a node.
Two common models you should know are property graphs and RDF triples.
Now look at the small example diagram.
It is written as plain text, so let me describe it.
At the top there is Patient A, with an arrow of type CONTACTED pointing to Patient B.
That reads as: Patient A contacted Patient B.
Beneath Patient A, there is an arrow of type VISITED pointing down to Clinic K.
So Patient A visited Clinic K.
Beneath Patient B, there is an arrow of type CONTACTED pointing down to Staff C.
So Patient B contacted Staff C.
Notice how the relationship types are written in capitals inside square brackets, and the nodes are written in round brackets.
This is a nice picture of how a contact-tracing style question can be stored directly as a network.
The source then makes an important point: relationships are first-class.
That means relationships are stored and treated as real, important objects in their own right, not something you only reconstruct later.
A graph traversal simply follows edges from one node to the next, instead of expressing every single hop as a join.
Now, be careful here.
Relational databases can also represent graphs.
They do it through adjacency tables, which store pairs of connected items, and through recursive common table expressions, or recursive CTEs, which let a query repeatedly follow those pairs.
So graph systems can simplify the modelling and can help with some traversal workloads, but the source is explicit that this does not guarantee universally faster queries.
It is a fit-for-purpose advantage, not a blanket promise.
Next, some graph terminology.
The degree of a node is the number of edges incident to it, meaning the number of edges touching it.
For directed graphs we split this into in-degree, the edges arriving at the node, and out-degree, the edges leaving it.
A path is a sequence of connected nodes and edges, so it is a route you can walk from one node to another.
A shortest path is the path that minimises either the number of hops or, where edges carry weights, the total weight.
Connected components identify groups of nodes that can reach one another, in other words reachable groups.
Centrality estimates structural importance, that is, how important a node is because of where it sits in the network.
Then two algorithm points.
Breadth-first search finds shortest paths measured in hops, but in unweighted graphs, where every edge counts the same.
When edges carry weights, you need an appropriate algorithm, and the source names Dijkstra for the case where the weights are nonnegative.
So remember: breadth-first search for unweighted hop counts, Dijkstra for weighted paths with nonnegative weights.
Finally, knowledge graphs.
A knowledge graph represents entities and the semantic relationships between them, meaning relationships that carry real meaning.
It often uses ontologies, RDF subject-predicate-object triples, and the query language SPARQL.
Each triple has three parts: a subject, a predicate and an object, for example a patient, a relationship, and a clinic.
Property graphs, by contrast, often use Cypher or Gremlin as their query languages.
An ontology defines concepts, relationships and constraints, and it supports interoperability between systems and inference, which means drawing new conclusions from what is already stated.
The section closes with a warning: a knowledge graph is not merely any graph visualisation.
A pretty picture of dots and lines is not enough; what makes it a knowledge graph is the meaningful, structured representation of entities and their semantic relationships.
